evidence.source: Hong Kong Educational University, Lexicon of Chinese Phonology: Richi (貴)
evidence.text: The page presents oracle-bone, bronze, seal, and standard forms. Its written explanation describes the forms as hands holding earth and analyzes 貝 as the semantic element and 中 as the phonetic element. This is an account from that reference; its proposed 中 phonetic analysis differs from the traditional 臾 analysis.
evidence.title: 字源考釋 - 貴

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, transcribing 說文解字 and Duan Yucai's commentary
evidence.text: The transmitted 說文 entry glosses 貴 as “not cheap” and analyzes it as 从貝臾聲, adding 臾，古文蕢. Duan's annotation gives the fanqie 居胃切. This establishes what the historical dictionary asserts; it does not independently confirm that the early graph depicted the same components.
evidence.title: 說文解字「貴」

evidence.source: Kim Jun-su, Korea Journal of Chinese Linguistics (2016), article record and abstract
evidence.text: The abstract argues 貴 and 遺 have different graphic and phonological origins and says 貴 is 貝 plus 臾, described as the protoform of 簣, as phonetic. It proposes Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese *kluds for 貴 and reports a modified Baxter–Sagart proposal *kut-s. The source presents competing reconstruction-system results; neither is a direct attestation of ancient pronunciation.
evidence.title: 《說文解字》貴聲系字의 上古音 再構에 대한 小考

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary's editorial notes trace several later variant spellings. It treats 䝿 as a direct regularization of the small-seal form and discusses other shapes as graphic variants or possible corruptions. One note explicitly warns that an old form of 蕢 was later misread in some dictionaries as an ancient form of 貴; 說文 itself says 臾 is an ancient form of 蕢. These notes concern later transmitted variants, not proof of the original graph's depiction.
evidence.title: A03945 貴 - 教育部《異體字字典》

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No primary inscription corpus entry was opened to establish the earliest attested spelling or sense of 貴; do not infer that date from dictionary ordering or search-result snippets.
The claimed Warring States phrase 黃金之貴 and the Zuozhuan market-price example remain unverified leads here. Their textual date, manuscript witness, and exact graph usage need primary-source checking.

Early graphic analyses conflict: one opened educational reference describes hands holding earth and calls 貝 semantic, 中 phonetic; 說文 instead gives 貝 semantic and 臾 phonetic. The evidence accessed here does not resolve the original depiction or phonetic component; no glyph image was visually inspected.

The dossier's *kluds is consistent with the opened 2016 paper's Zhengzhang proposal. That paper also reports a different Baxter–Sagart proposal *kut-s. I did not verify the reconstruction from the primary reconstruction publications or establish an uncontested Old Chinese value.

The role of 臾 as a sound component is asserted by 說文 and the 2016 study, but a complete reading-by-reading historical correspondence series for 臾 and 貴 was not independently compiled. Modern Mandarin guì and Cantonese gwai3 are dossier readings, not externally verified here.

The path from “not cheap/high price” to social rank, worth, esteem, or honor is semantically plausible and later dictionaries list such meanings, but dated evidence establishing each extension was not inspected.

The dossier's simplified form 贵 is acknowledged as the current counterpart of 貴, but the exact official adoption record and a dated pre-1956 attestation of this shape were not established in accessible pages.

No independent loanword analysis was found or needed to account for the supported formation claims; the Tibetan comparison in the dossier was not verified and should not be treated as demonstrated etymology.

No primary inscription corpus entry or artifact image was opened to establish the earliest attestation of 貴 or its earliest use. Search-result claims that it first appears in bronze inscriptions and occurs in a Warring States tomb phrase remain unverified.

The early graphic interpretation is disputed: the Hong Kong Educational University reference describes hands holding earth and assigns 中 as phonetic; 說文 and the 2016 phonology study analyze 貝 plus 臾. The evidence gathered does not resolve the original depiction or establish which account best explains early forms.

The role of 臾 is well-attested as a traditional dictionary and scholarly analysis, and the 2016 abstract associates it with the protoform of 簣. Its exact historical sound correspondence to 貴 is not fully established by a comparative series in this research. In Zhengzhang Shangfang’s system the study reports 貴 *kluds and series member 匱 *gruds, 蕢 *gruds / *kʰruːds, and 臾 *gruds; it separately reports modified Baxter–Sagart 貴 *kut-s and 匱 *grut-s. No direct ancient pronunciation is known.

No independently dated primary lexical attestations were inspected. Classical quotations reported by a secondary dictionary suggest price, rank, and esteem/value uses, but they do not establish the chronology or semantic pathway among these senses.

The modern readings Mandarin guì/gui4 and Cantonese gwai3 are externally listed, but a same-system historical reconstruction for both 貴 and the proposed phonetic component was not independently assembled.
The 1956 general simplification date is reported by the official search result, but the exact official table entry for 贵 and a pre-1956 attestation of this exact form were not verified.

No historical glyph candidates are included because Commons search did not establish a candidate with sufficiently clear identity and reuse provenance, and Xiaoxuetang’s character-specific direct image query was inaccessible. No image pixels were inspected.

The dossier’s Tibetan comparison was not verified; it should not be treated as established etymology. No whole-character phonetic-loan proposal was confirmed, and the early-form dispute concerns graphic analysis rather than a demonstrated borrowing.
No historical reconstruction or period-specific reading for 中 in the proposed 貴 analysis was found; the available historical reconstructions concern 貴 and the traditional 臾 series, not 中.

The local modern Mandarin pair 中 zhōng and 貴 guì does not establish a historical phonetic relation. No Modern Mandarin pronunciation card is warranted by this component-specific task unless the interface explicitly permits reporting a nonmatching pair as contrastive only.

Official Unicode character-specific Unihan pages were attempted at the prescribed URLs but were inaccessible through the browser tool; local rows were inspected, but no accessible official click-through record was verified.

limitations.text: No glyph candidate could be selected: the researched candidates did not establish a verifiable 貴 image with a clear form label and usable image rights. The early graph’s depiction and analysis remain disputed.
